Reference: Bajari, Benkard and Levin (2007)

Model Setting

The paper asks how to estimate the structural parameters of a dynamic game (entry and exit costs, investment costs, the distribution of private shocks) when computing a Markov perfect equilibrium even once is close to prohibitive and when the game may have many equilibria. It proposes a two-step estimator that never solves the model. In the first step the econometrician estimates the agents' policy functions and the law of motion of the state variables directly from the data; because agents in equilibrium hold correct beliefs, this step recovers their equilibrium beliefs. Forward simulation then turns the estimated policies and transitions into estimates of value functions, both for the observed policy and for any alternative policy. In the second step the remaining parameters are chosen so that the observed policy is a best response: the equilibrium conditions are written as a system of inequalities saying that the observed policy is weakly preferred to every alternative, and a simulated minimum distance estimator minimizes the squared violations of these inequalities. The approach builds on Hotz and Miller (1993) and Hotz, Miller, Sanders and Smith (1994), but unlike the contemporaneous estimators of Aguirregabiria and Mira (2007), Pakes, Ostrovsky and Berry (2007) and Pesendorfer and Schmidt-Dengler (2003), it handles continuous controls (investment, prices) together with discrete ones (entry, exit) in a unified framework, which makes it applicable to the Ericson and Pakes (1995) class of models. It also extends with little change to models that are only set identified, where it delivers bounds and confidence regions.

Two results organize the paper. First, when per-period profits are linear in the unknown parameters, value functions are linear in them too, so the expensive simulation is done once and each candidate parameter only rescales the simulated terms. Second, under a parametric (or discrete nonparametric) first stage the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, with a variance driven entirely by first-stage sampling error because simulation error vanishes asymptotically. Monte Carlo experiments on a machine replacement problem in the spirit of Rust (1987) and on a Pakes and McGuire (1994) style oligopoly with entry, exit and investment show that the estimator works with as few as 100 to 400 observations, with each round of estimation of the oligopoly model taking under a minute.

The Dynamic Game

There are NNN firms i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,Ni=1,…,N and discrete time t=1,2,…,∞t=1,2,\ldots,\inftyt=1,2,…,∞. A commonly observed vector of state variables st∈S⊂RL\mathbf{s}_t\in S\subset\mathbb{R}^Lst​∈S⊂RL summarizes conditions at ttt (capacities, market shares, the set of incumbents). Firms choose actions ait∈Aia_{it}\in A_iait​∈Ai​ simultaneously, with at=(a1t,…,aNt)∈A\mathbf{a}_t=(a_{1t},\ldots,a_{Nt})\in Aat​=(a1t​,…,aNt​)∈A. Before acting, firm iii receives a private shock νit\nu_{it}νit​, drawn independently across firms and over time from a distribution Gi(⋅∣st)G_i(\cdot\mid\mathbf{s}_t)Gi​(⋅∣st​) with support Vi⊂RM\mathcal{V}_i\subset\mathbb{R}^MVi​⊂RM; the vector of shocks is νt=(ν1t,…,νNt)\boldsymbol{\nu}_t=(\nu_{1t},\ldots,\nu_{Nt})νt​=(ν1t​,…,νNt​). Per-period profits are πi(at,st,νit)\pi_i(\mathbf{a}_t,\mathbf{s}_t,\nu_{it})πi​(at​,st​,νit​), and firms share a discount factor β<1\beta<1β<1. The next state is drawn from the transition distribution P(st+1∣at,st)P(\mathbf{s}_{t+1}\mid\mathbf{a}_t,\mathbf{s}_t)P(st+1​∣at​,st​), so current actions such as entry, exit or investment shape the future strategic environment. A Markov strategy is a function σi:S×Vi→Ai\sigma_i:S\times\mathcal{V}_i\rightarrow A_iσi​:S×Vi​→Ai​, and a profile is σ=(σ1,…,σN)\boldsymbol{\sigma}=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_N)σ=(σ1​,…,σN​) (the paper prints the last subscript as a lowercase nnn). Given a profile σ\boldsymbol{\sigma}σ, the ex ante value function of firm iii, evaluated before the private shocks are realized, satisfies the recursion:

Vi(s;σ)=Eν[πi(σ(s,ν),s,νi)+β∫Vi(s′;σ) dP(s′∣σ(s,ν),s)  ∣  s](1)V_i(\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\sigma})=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\left[\pi_i(\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{s},\boldsymbol{\nu}),\mathbf{s},\nu_i)+\beta\int V_i(\mathbf{s}';\boldsymbol{\sigma})\,dP(\mathbf{s}'\mid\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{s},\boldsymbol{\nu}),\mathbf{s})\;\Big|\;\mathbf{s}\right] \tag{1}Vi​(s;σ)=Eν​[πi​(σ(s,ν),s,νi​)+β∫Vi​(s′;σ)dP(s′∣σ(s,ν),s)​s](1)

and ViV_iVi​ is assumed bounded for every profile. The profile σ\boldsymbol{\sigma}σ is a (pure strategy) Markov perfect equilibrium (MPE) if for all firms iii, states s\mathbf{s}s and alternative Markov strategies σi′\sigma_i'σi′​:

Vi(s;σ)≥Vi(s;σi′,σ−i)(2)V_i(\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\sigma})\geq V_i(\mathbf{s};\sigma_i',\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i}) \tag{2}Vi​(s;σ)≥Vi​(s;σi′​,σ−i​)(2)

where the right-hand side is defined by the same recursion with firm iii playing σi′\sigma_i'σi′​ against σ−i\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i}σ−i​. Existence of an MPE is assumed (Doraszelski and Satterthwaite 2007 give conditions in a related model), and there may be many. The primitives are β\betaβ, the profit functions, the transition PPP and the shock distributions G1,…,GNG_1,\ldots,G_NG1​,…,GN​. The discount factor is treated as known, PPP is estimated directly from observed transitions, and profits and shock distributions are known up to a finite parameter vector θ\thetaθ, written πi(a,s,νi;θ)\pi_i(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{s},\nu_i;\theta)πi​(a,s,νi​;θ) and Gi(νi∣s;θ)G_i(\nu_i\mid\mathbf{s};\theta)Gi​(νi​∣s;θ). The goal is to recover the true value θ0\theta_0θ0​.

Two Running Examples

The first example is dynamic discrete choice, with a single agent as a special case: the action set is finite and the shock is a vector of choice-specific shocks that enter profits additively. The leading case is the machine replacement problem of Rust (1987). The state sss is the age of a machine; the manager either replaces it (a=1a=1a=1) or maintains it (a=0a=0a=0), in which case it ages by one period up to a maximum age. Per-period profit is:

π(a,s,ν;θ)={−μs+ν(0)if a=0−R+ν(1)if a=1(3)\pi(a,s,\nu;\theta)=\begin{cases}-\mu s+\nu(0) & \text{if } a=0\\ -R+\nu(1) & \text{if } a=1\end{cases} \tag{3}π(a,s,ν;θ)={−μs+ν(0)−R+ν(1)​if a=0if a=1​(3)

with θ=(μ,R)\theta=(\mu,R)θ=(μ,R), where μs−ν(0)\mu s-\nu(0)μs−ν(0) is the maintenance cost and R−ν(1)R-\nu(1)R−ν(1) the replacement cost. The optimal policy is a cutoff rule: σ(s,ν)=1\sigma(s,\nu)=1σ(s,ν)=1 if and only if ν(1)−ν(0)≥η(s)\nu(1)-\nu(0)\geq\eta(s)ν(1)−ν(0)≥η(s), with η(⋅)\eta(\cdot)η(⋅) decreasing in age.

The second example is a dynamic oligopoly in the tradition of Ericson and Pakes (1995) and Pakes and McGuire (1994). Each incumbent has a state zit∈{1,2,…,zˉ}z_{it}\in\{1,2,\ldots,\bar{z}\}zit​∈{1,2,…,zˉ} (quality, capital or productivity), and potential entrants have zit=0z_{it}=0zit​=0. An incumbent chooses investment Iit≥0I_{it}\geq0Iit​≥0 to improve its own state stochastically, and earns in period ttt:

qit(pit−mc(qit,st;μ))−C(Iit,νit;ξ)(4)q_{it}\left(p_{it}-mc(q_{it},\mathbf{s}_t;\mu)\right)-C(I_{it},\nu_{it};\xi) \tag{4}qit​(pit​−mc(qit​,st​;μ))−C(Iit​,νit​;ξ)(4)

where pitp_{it}pit​ is its price, qit=qi(st,pt;λ)q_{it}=q_i(\mathbf{s}_t,\mathbf{p}_t;\lambda)qit​=qi​(st​,pt​;λ) its quantity, mc(⋅)mc(\cdot)mc(⋅) marginal cost, C(⋅)C(\cdot)C(⋅) the cost of investment with private shock νit\nu_{it}νit​, and λ,μ,ξ\lambda,\mu,\xiλ,μ,ξ are parameters. Prices and quantities do not affect the evolution of the state, so they are determined in a static spot-market equilibrium given st\mathbf{s}_tst​. An incumbent may exit at the end of the period and collect a scrap value ϕ\phiϕ. One randomly selected potential entrant may enter at a privately observed cost νet\nu_{et}νet​ drawn from GeG_eGe​. Incumbents use an investment strategy Ii(s,νi)I_i(\mathbf{s},\nu_i)Ii​(s,νi​) and an exit strategy χi(s,νi)\chi_i(\mathbf{s},\nu_i)χi​(s,νi​), and the entrant uses χe(s,νe)\chi_e(\mathbf{s},\nu_e)χe​(s,νe​), entering when the expected profit from doing so exceeds its entry cost. The paper focuses on symmetric equilibria, in which a strategy depends on the firm's own state and is invariant to permutations of rivals' states.

First Stage: Policy Functions and State Transitions

The data contain actions at\mathbf{a}_tat​ and the complete state st\mathbf{s}_tst​ for one market or a set of similar markets. The key maintained assumption is equilibrium selection (Assumption ES): the data are generated by a single MPE profile σ\boldsymbol{\sigma}σ. This is weak if the equilibrium is unique and stronger when pooling markets, where it requires the same equilibrium to be played everywhere. Transition probabilities are estimated parametrically (for example by maximum likelihood) or by observed frequencies when states and actions are few. Policy functions are harder because they depend on unobserved shocks, and the paper treats two leading cases.

Discrete choice. Under Assumption DC, Ai={0,1,…,Ki}A_i=\{0,1,\ldots,K_i\}Ai​={0,1,…,Ki​}, the shock is a vector (νi(ai))ai∈Ai(\nu_i(a_i))_{a_i\in A_i}(νi​(ai​))ai​∈Ai​​ and profits are additively separable, πi(a,s,νi)=π~i(a,s)+νi(ai)\pi_i(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{s},\nu_i)=\tilde{\pi}_i(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{s})+\nu_i(a_i)πi​(a,s,νi​)=π~i​(a,s)+νi​(ai​). Define the choice-specific value function:

vi(ai′,s)−vi(ai,s)=ln⁡(Pr⁡(ai′∣s))−ln⁡(Pr⁡(ai∣s))(7)v_i(a_i',\mathbf{s})-v_i(a_i,\mathbf{s})=\ln\left(\Pr(a_i'\mid\mathbf{s})\right)-\ln\left(\Pr(a_i\mid\mathbf{s})\right) \tag{7}vi​(ai′​,s)−vi​(ai​,s)=ln(Pr(ai′​∣s))−ln(Pr(ai​∣s))(7)

where Pr⁡(ai∣s)\Pr(a_i\mid\mathbf{s})Pr(ai​∣s) is the probability of choice aia_iai​ in state s\mathbf{s}s. Only differences are recovered (levels need a normalization such as vi(0,s)=0v_i(0,\mathbf{s})=0vi​(0,s)=0), but differences suffice for the policy rule. If the shock distribution contains unknown parameters, the policy is recovered as a function of them. With large state spaces, state-by-state inversion is noisy, so one smooths across states with flexible parametric forms or kernels and imposes restrictions such as symmetry.

Continuous choice. Under Assumption MC (monotone choice), Ai,Vi⊂RA_i,\mathcal{V}_i\subset\mathbb{R}Ai​,Vi​⊂R and πi(a,s,νi)\pi_i(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{s},\nu_i)πi​(a,s,νi​) has increasing differences in (ai,νi)(a_i,\nu_i)(ai​,νi​), which is equivalent to ∂2πi/(∂ai∂νi)≥0\partial^2\pi_i/(\partial a_i\partial\nu_i)\geq0∂2πi​/(∂ai​∂νi​)≥0 when πi\pi_iπi​ is twice differentiable. By Topkis' theorem the optimal policy σi(s,νi)\sigma_i(\mathbf{s},\nu_i)σi​(s,νi​) is increasing in νi\nu_iνi​. Let Fi(ai∣s)F_i(a_i\mid\mathbf{s})Fi​(ai​∣s) be the observed distribution of firm iii's action at state s\mathbf{s}s. Monotonicity maps quantiles of the shock into quantiles of the action:

Fi(ai∣s)=Gi(σi−1(ai;s)∣s;θ)⟹σi(s,νi)=Fi−1(Gi(νi∣s;θ)∣s)(8)F_i(a_i\mid\mathbf{s})=G_i\left(\sigma_i^{-1}(a_i;\mathbf{s})\mid\mathbf{s};\theta\right)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sigma_i(\mathbf{s},\nu_i)=F_i^{-1}\left(G_i(\nu_i\mid\mathbf{s};\theta)\mid\mathbf{s}\right) \tag{8}Fi​(ai​∣s)=Gi​(σi−1​(ai​;s)∣s;θ)⟹σi​(s,νi​)=Fi−1​(Gi​(νi​∣s;θ)∣s)(8)

For instance, if investment shocks are N(0,σ2)N(0,\sigma^2)N(0,σ2), the investment policy is obtained by inverting the estimated F(I∣s)F(I\mid\mathbf{s})F(I∣s) and evaluating it at Φ(νi/σ)\Phi(\nu_i/\sigma)Φ(νi​/σ), with Φ\PhiΦ the standard normal distribution function. This matching of quantiles is the new element relative to the discrete choice literature. When firms make several choices with several shocks, the method applies if the decisions separate cleanly; if several shocks enter one policy function, that policy may not be identified from the data. Policies and transitions are estimable only on the support of the data, and value functions additionally need all states reachable from s\mathbf{s}s in equilibrium; for unvisited states one either extrapolates parametrically or drops the corresponding equilibrium conditions in the second stage.

First Stage: Forward Simulation of Value Functions

For any profile σ\boldsymbol{\sigma}σ and parameter θ\thetaθ, the value function is:

Vi(s;σ;θ)=E[∑t=0∞βtπi(σ(st,νt),st,νit;θ)  ∣  s0=s;θ](9)V_i(\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\sigma};\theta)=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^t\pi_i(\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{s}_t,\boldsymbol{\nu}_t),\mathbf{s}_t,\nu_{it};\theta)\;\Big|\;\mathbf{s}_0=\mathbf{s};\theta\right] \tag{9}Vi​(s;σ;θ)=E[t=0∑∞​βtπi​(σ(st​,νt​),st​,νit​;θ)​s0​=s;θ](9)

Given the estimated transition P^\hat{P}P^, a path is simulated by forward simulation: starting at s0=s\mathbf{s}_0=\mathbf{s}s0​=s, draw νi0\nu_{i0}νi0​ from Gi(⋅∣s0,θ)G_i(\cdot\mid\mathbf{s}_0,\theta)Gi​(⋅∣s0​,θ) for each firm; compute actions ai0=σi(s0,νi0)a_{i0}=\sigma_i(\mathbf{s}_0,\nu_{i0})ai0​=σi​(s0​,νi0​) and profits πi(a0,s0,νi0;θ)\pi_i(\mathbf{a}_0,\mathbf{s}_0,\nu_{i0};\theta)πi​(a0​,s0​,νi0​;θ); draw s1\mathbf{s}_1s1​ from P^(⋅∣a0,s0)\hat{P}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{a}_0,\mathbf{s}_0)P^(⋅∣a0​,s0​); and repeat for TTT periods or until every firm reaches a terminal state such as exit. Averaging discounted profits over many paths gives V^i(s;σ;θ)\hat{V}_i(\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\sigma};\theta)V^i​(s;σ;θ). Evaluated at the first-stage policy σ^\hat{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}σ^ it estimates the equilibrium payoff, and evaluated at (σi′,σ^−i)(\sigma_i',\hat{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-i})(σi′​,σ^−i​) it estimates the payoff from a deviation against the estimated rival behavior. Unlike Hotz, Miller, Sanders and Smith (1994), who simulate states and actions directly and rely on the logit structure, the procedure draws states and shocks and computes actions.

The simulation would have to be repeated for each candidate θ\thetaθ, except in one important case. If the shock distributions are known and profits are linear in parameters, with Ψi\Psi_iΨi​ an MMM-dimensional vector of basis functions, then:

The vector Wi=(Wi1,…,WiM)\mathbf{W}_i=(W_i^1,\ldots,W_i^M)Wi​=(Wi1​,…,WiM​) of expected discounted basis functions does not depend on θ\thetaθ, so it is simulated once per policy and ViV_iVi​ is then available for every θ\thetaθ by a single inner product. Entry costs, scrap values, fixed costs, investment costs and marginal costs typically enter profits linearly. Linearity can survive unknown shock parameters (if νit\nu_{it}νit​ is N(μ,κ2)N(\mu,\kappa^2)N(μ,κ2) and profits contain aitνita_{it}\nu_{it}ait​νit​, write the term as ait(μ+κωit)a_{it}(\mu+\kappa\omega_{it})ait​(μ+κωit​) with ωit\omega_{it}ωit​ standard normal), and if ViV_iVi​ is linear in only some parameters one can nest an inner optimization over the linear parameters inside an outer search over the others.

Second Stage: Equilibrium Inequalities and Minimum Distance

Assumption S1 requires that the policy functions σi(s,νi;α)\sigma_i(\mathbf{s},\nu_i;\alpha)σi​(s,νi​;α) and transitions P(st+1∣st,at;α)P(\mathbf{s}_{t+1}\mid\mathbf{s}_t,\mathbf{a}_t;\alpha)P(st+1​∣st​,at​;α) be indexed by a finite vector α\alphaα with a first-stage estimator satisfying n(α^n−α0)→dN(0,Vα)\sqrt{n}(\hat{\alpha}_n-\alpha_0)\rightarrow_dN(0,V_\alpha)n​(α^n​−α0​)→d​N(0,Vα​). This covers a nonparametric first stage with discrete actions and states, or a parametric one with continuous actions and states, but not a nonparametric first stage with continuous actions or states. The parameters that rationalize σ\boldsymbol{\sigma}σ as an MPE of the game defined by PPP and θ\thetaθ form the set:

Θ0(σ,P):={θ:  Vi(s;σi,σ−i;θ)≥Vi(s;σi′,σ−i;θ)  for all s,i,σi′}(11)\Theta_0(\boldsymbol{\sigma},P):=\left\{\theta:\;V_i(\mathbf{s};\sigma_i,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i};\theta)\geq V_i(\mathbf{s};\sigma_i',\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i};\theta)\ \text{ for all } \mathbf{s},i,\sigma_i'\right\} \tag{11}Θ0​(σ,P):={θ:Vi​(s;σi​,σ−i​;θ)≥Vi​(s;σi′​,σ−i​;θ)  for all s,i,σi′​}(11)

Asymptotic Theory for Identified Models

Assumption S2 has five parts: (i) X1,…,XnI∈XX_1,\ldots,X_{n_I}\in\mathcal{X}X1​,…,XnI​​∈X are i.i.d. draws from HHH; (ii) for each XkX_kXk​ the simulator uses independent draws, is unbiased, EV^i=Vi<∞\mathbb{E}\hat{V}_i=V_i<\inftyEV^i​=Vi​<∞, and is smooth (twice differentiable in θ\thetaθ and α\alphaα, three times in θ\thetaθ) with probability one; (iii) as n→∞n\rightarrow\inftyn→∞, both ns,nI→∞n_s,n_I\rightarrow\inftyns​,nI​→∞ and n/ns2→0n/n_s^2\rightarrow0n/ns2​→0; (iv) Θ⊂RM\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^MΘ⊂RM is compact and θ0=arg⁡min⁡θ∈ΘQ(θ,α0)\theta_0=\arg\min_{\theta\in\Theta}Q(\theta,\alpha_0)θ0​=argminθ∈Θ​Q(θ,α0​) (identification); (v) there is a full-rank matrix B0B_0B0​ such that, for θ\thetaθ near θ0\theta_0θ0​:

∂∂θQn(θ,α^n)=∂∂θQn(θ0,α^n)+(B0+op(1))(θ−θ0)(16)\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}Q_n(\theta,\hat{\alpha}_n)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}Q_n(\theta_0,\hat{\alpha}_n)+\left(B_0+o_p(1)\right)(\theta-\theta_0) \tag{16}∂θ∂​Qn​(θ,α^n​)=∂θ∂​Qn​(θ0​,α^n​)+(B0​+op​(1))(θ−θ0​)(16)

Typically B0=B(θ0)B_0=B(\theta_0)B0​=B(θ0​) with B(θ)≡∂2Q(θ,α0)/∂θ∂θ′B(\theta)\equiv\partial^2Q(\theta,\alpha_0)/\partial\theta\partial\theta'B(θ)≡∂2Q(θ,α0​)/∂θ∂θ′, which requires HHH to sample inequalities smoothly. The same draws may be used for the two value functions within one inequality, which is desirable because the positive correlation lowers simulation variance. Proposition 1 states that under Assumptions S1 and S2:

n(θ^−θ0)→dN(0,  B0−1Λ0VαΛ0′B0−1),Λ0≡∂2∂θ∂α′Q(θ,α)∣θ=θ0,α=α0(17)\sqrt{n}\left(\hat{\theta}-\theta_0\right)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\;B_0^{-1}\Lambda_0V_\alpha\Lambda_0'B_0^{-1}\right),\qquad\Lambda_0\equiv\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta\partial\alpha'}Q(\theta,\alpha)\Big|_{\theta=\theta_0,\alpha=\alpha_0} \tag{17}n​(θ^−θ0​)d​N(0,B0−1​Λ0​Vα​Λ0′​B0−1​),Λ0​≡∂θ∂α′∂2​Q(θ,α)​θ=θ0​,α=α0​​(17)

The asymptotics are in the number of first-stage observations nnn, since nIn_InI​ and nsn_sns​ are under the researcher's control. The proof first shows uniform convergence, sup⁡θ∈Θ∣Qn(θ,α^n)−Q(θ,α0)∣=op(1)\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|Q_n(\theta,\hat{\alpha}_n)-Q(\theta,\alpha_0)|=o_p(1)supθ∈Θ​∣Qn​(θ,α^n​)−Q(θ,α0​)∣=op​(1), which with identification gives consistency. For the distribution, the scaled gradient n ∂Qn(θ0,α^n)/∂θ\sqrt{n}\,\partial Q_n(\theta_0,\hat{\alpha}_n)/\partial\thetan​∂Qn​(θ0​,α^n​)/∂θ is split into four terms. The first is the first-stage sampling error; a mean-value expansion in α\alphaα gives a term that behaves like Λ0n(α^n−α0)\Lambda_0\sqrt{n}(\hat{\alpha}_n-\alpha_0)Λ0​n​(α^n​−α0​). The second is simulation variance, mean zero and independent across inequalities, which disappears as nIn_InI​ and nsn_sns​ grow. The third is simulation bias, which arises because the criterion is nonlinear in g^\hat{g}g^​; its expectation is proportional to the variance of g^\hat{g}g^​ and so shrinks at rate nsn_sns​, which is why nsn_sns​ must grow faster than n\sqrt{n}n​. The fourth, the usual second-stage sampling term, is identically zero because the criterion and its derivative vanish at the truth for every inequality: there is no sampling error in the second stage. Hence:

n ∂∂θQn(θ0,α^n)→dN(0,  Λ0VαΛ0′)(18)\sqrt{n}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}Q_n(\theta_0,\hat{\alpha}_n)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\;\Lambda_0V_\alpha\Lambda_0'\right) \tag{18}n​∂θ∂​Qn​(θ0​,α^n​)d​N(0,Λ0​Vα​Λ0′​)(18)

and inverting the expansion in part (v) gives the proposition. Standard errors therefore reflect only first-stage sampling error, transmitted through Λ0\Lambda_0Λ0​. Because Λ0\Lambda_0Λ0​ is hard to express in terms of primitives (the first-stage parameters enter the WWW terms in a complex way), the paper recommends subsampling or the bootstrap. In finite samples θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ need not rationalize the estimated policies exactly as an equilibrium: some inequalities remain violated, which is typical of two-step estimators and one motivation for the iterative procedure of Aguirregabiria and Mira (2007).

Bounds Estimation for Set-Identified Models

When the model is only set identified, parts (i), (iv) and (v) of Assumption S2 and the requirement nI→∞n_I\rightarrow\inftynI​→∞ are dropped, and a fixed set of inequalities x1,…,xnIx_1,\ldots,x_{n_I}x1​,…,xnI​​ is used. Let ΘnI(σ,P)\Theta_{n_I}(\boldsymbol{\sigma},P)ΘnI​​(σ,P) be the set of θ\thetaθ that satisfy these nIn_InI​ inequalities; then Θ0⊆ΘnI\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta_{n_I}Θ0​⊆ΘnI​​, with equality if they are the full set of equilibrium conditions. Following Manski and Tamer (2002), the set estimator collects all parameters that nearly minimize the same criterion:

Θ^n≡{θ:  Qn(θ,α^n)≤min⁡θ′∈ΘQn(θ′,α^n)+μn}(19)\hat{\Theta}_n\equiv\left\{\theta:\;Q_n(\theta,\hat{\alpha}_n)\leq\min_{\theta'\in\Theta}Q_n(\theta',\hat{\alpha}_n)+\mu_n\right\} \tag{19}Θ^n​≡{θ:Qn​(θ,α^n​)≤θ′∈Θmin​Qn​(θ′,α^n​)+μn​}(19)

for some μn>0\mu_n>0μn​>0 with μn→0\mu_n\rightarrow0μn​→0. With the one-sided distance ρ(Θ,Θ′)≡sup⁡θ∈Θinf⁡θ′∈Θ′∣θ−θ′∣\rho(\Theta,\Theta')\equiv\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\inf_{\theta'\in\Theta'}|\theta-\theta'|ρ(Θ,Θ′)≡supθ∈Θ​infθ′∈Θ′​∣θ−θ′∣, Proposition 2 states that under Assumptions S1 and S2(ii) and (iii):

ρ(Θ^n,ΘnI)→p0,andρ(ΘnI,Θ^n)→p0  if  sup⁡θ∈Θ∣Qn(θ,α^n)−Q(θ,α0)∣/μn→0(20)\rho\left(\hat{\Theta}_n,\Theta_{n_I}\right)\xrightarrow{p}0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad\rho\left(\Theta_{n_I},\hat{\Theta}_n\right)\xrightarrow{p}0\ \text{ if }\ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|Q_n(\theta,\hat{\alpha}_n)-Q(\theta,\alpha_0)\right|/\mu_n\rightarrow0 \tag{20}ρ(Θ^n​,ΘnI​​)p​0,andρ(ΘnI​​,Θ^n​)p​0  if  θ∈Θsup​∣Qn​(θ,α^n​)−Q(θ,α0​)∣/μn​→0(20)

The first part says every point of the estimated set is eventually close to the identified set and holds even with μn=0\mu_n=0μn​=0; the second says the whole identified set is eventually captured, which requires μn\mu_nμn​ to vanish slowly enough. When the inequalities are linear in parameters, Θ^n\hat{\Theta}_nΘ^n​ is a convex polyhedron and its computation is a linear programming problem (vertex enumeration, or the Gibbs sampler of Bajari and Benkard 2004 for uniform draws from the set); otherwise simulated annealing can be used. For inference the paper applies the subsampling procedure of Romano and Shaikh (2006a), an extension of Chernozhukov, Hong and Tamer (2007). Starting from a set Θ\ThetaΘ known to contain θ0\theta_0θ0​, the criterion Qn,bQ_{n,b}Qn,b​ is computed on BBB subsamples of size nbn_bnb​, and for each θ∈Θ\theta\in\Thetaθ∈Θ the critical value is:

c^n(0.95,θ)=inf⁡{c:  1B∑b=1B1{nbQn,b(θ,α^n)≤c}≥0.95}(21)\hat{c}_n(0.95,\theta)=\inf\left\{c:\;\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf{1}\left\{n_bQ_{n,b}(\theta,\hat{\alpha}_n)\leq c\right\}\geq0.95\right\} \tag{21}c^n​(0.95,θ)=inf{c:B1​b=1∑B​1{nb​Qn,b​(θ,α^n​)≤c}≥0.95}(21)

Θ^0.95={θ:  n⋅Qn(θ,α^n)≤c^n(0.95,θ)},lim inf⁡n→∞Pr⁡(θ∈Θ^0.95)≥0.95(22)\hat{\Theta}_{0.95}=\left\{\theta:\;n\cdot Q_n(\theta,\hat{\alpha}_n)\leq\hat{c}_n(0.95,\theta)\right\},\qquad\liminf_{n\rightarrow\infty}\Pr\left(\theta\in\hat{\Theta}_{0.95}\right)\geq0.95 \tag{22}Θ^0.95​={θ:n⋅Qn​(θ,α^n​)≤c^n​(0.95,θ)},n→∞liminf​Pr(θ∈Θ^0.95​)≥0.95(22)

for every θ\thetaθ in the identified set, hence in particular for θ0\theta_0θ0​. A confidence region for the identified set as a whole is larger and requires an iterative step-down procedure in which the critical value is computed from the supremum of the subsample criterion over the current set.

Unobserved State Variables and Related Estimators

The framework assumes that all commonly known states are observed, so independent private shocks are the only unobservables. The paper lists ways to relax this: recover the unobserved state in the first stage (product characteristics as in Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes 1995, or productivity as in Olley and Pakes 1996); with long panels, estimate policies market by market and pool inequalities in the second stage, which also allows different equilibria across markets; use parametric panel methods for the policy functions; follow Aguirregabiria and Mira (2007), who use the joint distribution of observed and unobserved states, although obtaining it seems to require computing an equilibrium; or use the EM approach of Arcidiacono and Miller (2007), which needs a second-stage likelihood.

Relative to the three contemporaneous extensions of Hotz and Miller to games, the paper states the following. Pesendorfer and Schmidt-Dengler (2003) apply the Hotz and Miller estimator most directly and provide identification results. Pakes, Ostrovsky and Berry (2007) build the second stage on pooled moment conditions instead of maximum likelihood. Aguirregabiria and Mira (2007) iterate the two-step estimator, regenerating choice probabilities from each round of estimates, which has attractive properties if it converges and can accommodate serially correlated unobserved states. All three are confined to discrete choice with an independent shock attached to each alternative, where value functions can be computed from choice probabilities by matrix algebra; the present estimator replaces matrix inversion by forward simulation, covers continuous choices, and uses inequalities so that it extends to set identification. The shared drawback of two-step methods is that the first stage ignores restrictions implied by the model, and first-stage noise causes finite-sample bias in a nonlinear second stage.

Monte Carlo: Machine Replacement

The design sets μ=1\mu=1μ=1, R=4R=4R=4, β=0.9\beta=0.9β=0.9, ages s∈{1,2,3,4,5}s\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}s∈{1,2,3,4,5}, and ν(0),ν(1)\nu(0),\nu(1)ν(0),ν(1) independent N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) with known distribution; samples have n=50,100,200,400n=50,100,200,400n=50,100,200,400 observations. The first stage is the replacement frequency at each of the five states. With v(1,s)=−R+βV(1;σ)v(1,s)=-R+\beta V(1;\sigma)v(1,s)=−R+βV(1;σ) and v(0,s)=−μs+βV(min⁡{s+1,5};σ)v(0,s)=-\mu s+\beta V(\min\{s+1,5\};\sigma)v(0,s)=−μs+βV(min{s+1,5};σ), the cutoff policy implies:

σ(s,ν)=1 ⇔ v(1,s)+ν(1)≥v(0,s)+ν(0),Pr⁡(a=1∣s)=Φ(v(1,s)−v(0,s)2)(23)\sigma(s,\nu)=1\ \Leftrightarrow\ v(1,s)+\nu(1)\geq v(0,s)+\nu(0),\qquad\Pr(a=1\mid s)=\Phi\left(\frac{v(1,s)-v(0,s)}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \tag{23}σ(s,ν)=1 ⇔ v(1,s)+ν(1)≥v(0,s)+ν(0),Pr(a=1∣s)=Φ(2​v(1,s)−v(0,s)​)(23)

Section 6.1 of the paper restates the profit function as a[−R−ν(1)]+(1−a)[−μs−ν(0)]a[-R-\nu(1)]+(1-a)[-\mu s-\nu(0)]a[−R−ν(1)]+(1−a)[−μs−ν(0)], with the shocks entering negatively, but its cutoff rule and value function decomposition treat them as additive, as in the earlier definition, which this note keeps. The value function is linear in θ\thetaθ:

V(s;σ;θ)=W1(s;σ)⋅R+W2(s;σ)⋅μ+W3(s;σ)=E[−∑t=0∞βtσ(st,νt)  ∣  s0=s]⋅R+E[−∑t=0∞βt(1−σ(st,νt))st  ∣  s0=s]⋅μ+E[∑t=0∞βtν(σ(st,νt))  ∣  s0=s](24)\begin{aligned} V(s;\sigma;\theta)&=W^1(s;\sigma)\cdot R+W^2(s;\sigma)\cdot\mu+W^3(s;\sigma)\\ &=\mathbb{E}\left[-\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^t\sigma(s_t,\nu_t)\;\Big|\;s_0=s\right]\cdot R+\mathbb{E}\left[-\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^t\left(1-\sigma(s_t,\nu_t)\right)s_t\;\Big|\;s_0=s\right]\cdot\mu\\ &\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^t\nu\left(\sigma(s_t,\nu_t)\right)\;\Big|\;s_0=s\right] \end{aligned} \tag{24}V(s;σ;θ)​=W1(s;σ)⋅R+W2(s;σ)⋅μ+W3(s;σ)=E[−t=0∑∞​βtσ(st​,νt​)​s0​=s]⋅R+E[−t=0∑∞​βt(1−σ(st​,νt​))st​​s0​=s]⋅μ+E[t=0∑∞​βtν(σ(st​,νt​))​s0​=s]​(24)

The three terms are the expected discounted number of replacements, the expected discounted maintenance burden, and the expected discounted value of the shocks attached to the chosen actions. Alternative policies are cutoff rules with cutoffs drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation 0.5 centered at the estimated cutoffs. Each design uses 500 Monte Carlo runs, nI=200n_I=200nI​=200 inequalities, and subsampled standard errors from 25 subsamples of size n/2n/2n/2.

  • n=200n=200n=200, ns=500n_s=500ns​=500: μ^\hat{\mu}μ^​ 0.99 (0.18, subsampled 0.17); R^\hat{R}R^ 4.00 (0.78, subsampled 0.86).

  • n=100n=100n=100, ns=250n_s=250ns​=250: μ^\hat{\mu}μ^​ 0.94 (0.32, subsampled 0.35); R^\hat{R}R^ 3.75 (1.26, subsampled 1.15).

  • n=50n=50n=50, ns=150n_s=150ns​=150: μ^\hat{\mu}μ^​ 0.89 (0.54, subsampled 0.47); R^\hat{R}R^ 3.57 (2.35, subsampled 2.27), with a 5 to 95 percent range for R^\hat{R}R^ of 0.60 to 8.16.

The paper reports t statistics of 12 to 20 at n=400n=400n=400 and 7 to 10 at n=100n=100n=100. The second stage takes about a third of the computing time of the first stage.

An Alternative Second Stage: Aggregate Moments

Because the inequality criterion is nonlinear in the first-stage estimates, first-stage noise biases the second stage. Following the suggestion of Pakes, Ostrovsky and Berry (2007) that aggregation averages out first-stage error, the paper considers a method of moments estimator. For each θ\thetaθ: simulate V^(s)\hat{V}(\mathbf{s})V^(s) at every observed state and every state reachable from one in a single period; use these values to compute the predicted entry probability, exit policy and investment of each incumbent at each observed state (which requires solving the optimal investment choice, analytic in this model); form moments as averages over states of observed minus predicted investment, entry and exit; and minimize a quadratic form in the moments. With VVV linear in θ\thetaθ the simulations are again done once. Three aggregate moments identify at most three parameters, so five more are added: the covariances of exit and of investment with the firm's own state, and the covariances of entry, exit and investment with the sum of rivals' states, for eight moments in total, with an optimal weight matrix when there are enough observations.

  • n=400n=400n=400: ξ^\hat{\xi}ξ^​ 1.01 (0.03), ϕ^\hat{\phi}ϕ^​ 6.09 (0.18), ν^L\hat{\nu}^Lν^L 7.04 (1.01), ν^H\hat{\nu}^Hν^H 11.1 (0.65).

  • n=200n=200n=200: 1.01 (0.05), 6.06 (0.24), 6.89 (1.98), 11.0 (1.54).

  • n=100n=100n=100: 1.01 (0.06), 6.02 (0.34), 6.86 (2.34), 11.1 (1.83).

The bias in the scrap value and in the lower bound of entry costs largely disappears even at n=100n=100n=100, while standard errors are smaller for ξ\xiξ and ϕ\phiϕ and, at n=200n=200n=200 and n=100n=100n=100, larger for the entry cost bounds, so there is no clear efficiency ranking. The paper's text attributes the bias reduction to the investment cost and the lower bound on the entry cost, although in its tables the investment cost has mean 1.01 under both estimators and the scrap value is what changes. The drawbacks are that the optimal continuous policy must be solved for (and simulated over private investment shocks in richer models) and that the approach does not extend to set-identified models; where the model is point identified and aggregate moments are easy to compute, the paper recommends considering both estimators.

This inequality is the definition of a pure-strategy Markov perfect equilibrium. The left-hand side is the value in equation (1) when every firm, including iii, follows the profile σ\boldsymbol{\sigma}σ. The right-hand side is the value firm iii obtains when it alone switches to another Markov strategy σi′\sigma_i'σi′​ while its rivals keep playing σ−i\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i}σ−i​; it solves the same recursion with σi′\sigma_i'σi′​ in place of σi\sigma_iσi​:

The condition must hold for every firm iii, every state s\mathbf{s}s and every alternative σi′\sigma_i'σi′​, so each σi\sigma_iσi​ is a best response to σ−i\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i}σ−i​ starting from any state: this is the perfection requirement. Restricting deviations to Markov strategies is without loss, because when rivals play Markov strategies firm iii faces a stationary Markov decision problem and has a Markov best response. The deviation changes firm iii's payoff in two ways: through current profit, and through the distribution of future states and hence of rivals' future actions.

For estimation the inequality is everything. The first stage estimates σ\boldsymbol{\sigma}σ and PPP, forward simulation (equations (9) and (10)) evaluates both sides for any θ\thetaθ, and the second stage looks for the θ\thetaθ at which the observed policy beats every alternative: the set in equation (11), the function ggg in equation (12) and the criterion in equation (13) are built directly from it. No equilibrium is ever computed, and multiplicity is harmless as long as the data come from one equilibrium (Assumption ES).

This is the per-period profit of the manager in the machine replacement example, a single-agent special case of the game. The state sss is the machine's age, a=1a=1a=1 means replace and a=0a=0a=0 means maintain. Maintaining costs μs−ν(0)\mu s-\nu(0)μs−ν(0), so μ>0\mu>0μ>0 is the maintenance cost per unit of age; replacing costs R−ν(1)R-\nu(1)R−ν(1), so R>0R>0R>0 is the replacement cost. The shocks ν(0),ν(1)\nu(0),\nu(1)ν(0),ν(1) are choice-specific, privately observed and enter additively with a positive sign: a large ν(a)\nu(a)ν(a) makes action aaa attractive this period. The form satisfies Assumption DC, with profit net of the shock equal to −μs-\mu s−μs for a=0a=0a=0 and −R-R−R for a=1a=1a=1.

The profit is linear in θ=(μ,R)\theta=(\mu,R)θ=(μ,R). Written in one line,

π(a,s,ν;θ)=−(1−a) s⋅μ−a⋅R+ν(a)\pi(a,s,\nu;\theta)=-(1-a)\,s\cdot\mu-a\cdot R+\nu(a)π(a,s,ν;θ)=−(1−a)s⋅μ−a⋅R+ν(a)

so the basis functions of equation (10) are −(1−a)s-(1-a)s−(1−a)s, −a-a−a and ν(a)\nu(a)ν(a), the last with a known coefficient of one. Discounting and averaging these three terms along simulated paths gives W2W^2W2, W1W^1W1 and W3W^3W3 in equation (24). The known coefficient on the shock fixes the scale of θ\thetaθ: the standard deviation of the shocks is the unit in which μ\muμ and RRR are measured.

The trade-off is dynamic. Replacing costs RRR today but resets the age to one, lowering future maintenance costs. The optimal policy is the cutoff rule ν(1)−ν(0)≥η(s)\nu(1)-\nu(0)\geq\eta(s)ν(1)−ν(0)≥η(s) with η(s)=v(0,s)−v(1,s)\eta(s)=v(0,s)-v(1,s)η(s)=v(0,s)−v(1,s), the difference of the choice-specific values in equation (23); older machines have a lower value of maintaining, so η\etaη falls with age. Section 6.1 of the paper restates the profit with −ν(1)-\nu(1)−ν(1) and −ν(0)-\nu(0)−ν(0). Since the shocks are symmetric around zero the two versions generate the same distribution of data, but only the positive-sign version here is literally consistent with the cutoff rule in equation (23) and with the positive sign of W3W^3W3 in equation (24).

This is the period profit of an incumbent in the dynamic oligopoly example. The first term is the static spot-market margin: quantity qitq_{it}qit​ times price minus marginal cost, where mc(qit,st;μ)mc(q_{it},\mathbf{s}_t;\mu)mc(qit​,st​;μ) is marginal cost with parameter μ\muμ and qit=qi(st,pt;λ)q_{it}=q_i(\mathbf{s}_t,\mathbf{p}_t;\lambda)qit​=qi​(st​,pt​;λ) comes from a demand system with parameter λ\lambdaλ. The second term is the cost of investment Iit≥0I_{it}\geq0Iit​≥0, with parameter ξ\xiξ and a private shock νit\nu_{it}νit​ to that cost.

The key structural assumption is a separation between static and dynamic decisions. Prices and quantities do not enter the transition of the state, so they are chosen to maximize current profit given st\mathbf{s}_tst​, and the first term reduces to a function of the state alone, the static equilibrium profit written later as π~i(st)\tilde{\pi}_i(\mathbf{s}_t)π~i​(st​). Investment is the only choice with intertemporal consequences besides entry and exit: it costs C(Iit,νit;ξ)C(I_{it},\nu_{it};\xi)C(Iit​,νit​;ξ) now and shifts the distribution of the firm's own future state zitz_{it}zit​. If a higher νit\nu_{it}νit​ lowers the marginal cost of investing, profit has increasing differences in (Iit,νit)(I_{it},\nu_{it})(Iit​,νit​) and Assumption MC applies, so the investment policy can be recovered by the quantile matching in equation (8).

The separation also organizes estimation. The parameters λ\lambdaλ and μ\muμ are estimated by static methods and placed in the first-stage vector α\alphaα, while ξ\xiξ, the scrap value ϕ\phiϕ and the entry cost distribution GeG_eGe​ require the dynamic model and form θ\thetaθ. In the Monte Carlo the expression is specialized to logit demand (equation (25)), constant marginal cost, and C(Ii)=ξIiC(I_i)=\xi I_iC(Ii​)=ξIi​ without a shock (equation (26)), which makes the incumbent value linear in (ξ,ϕ)(\xi,\phi)(ξ,ϕ) as in equation (28). Exit and entry payoffs are not in this expression: an exiting incumbent also collects ϕ\phiϕ, and an entrant pays νet\nu_{et}νet​.

Two things follow. The policy depends on the viv_ivi​ only through their differences across actions, so a normalization such as vi(0,s)=0v_i(0,\mathbf{s})=0vi​(0,s)=0 costs nothing. And integrating the rule over the distribution of νi\nu_iνi​ gives the conditional choice probabilities

Pr⁡(ai∣s)=Pr⁡(vi(ai,s)+νi(ai)≥vi(ai′,s)+νi(ai′)  ∀ai′∈Ai)\Pr(a_i\mid\mathbf{s})=\Pr\left(v_i(a_i,\mathbf{s})+\nu_i(a_i)\geq v_i(a_i',\mathbf{s})+\nu_i(a_i')\ \ \forall a_i'\in A_i\right)Pr(ai​∣s)=Pr(vi​(ai​,s)+νi​(ai​)≥vi​(ai′​,s)+νi​(ai′​)  ∀ai′​∈Ai​)

which are observed in the data. Inverting this map from value differences to probabilities, as in equation (7) for logit and equation (23) for normal shocks, recovers the policy rule without solving the model.

Start from the choice rule in equation (6) and suppose the shocks νi(ai)\nu_i(a_i)νi​(ai​) are independent across actions with the standard type 1 extreme value (Gumbel) distribution, whose distribution function is exp⁡(−e−ν)\exp(-e^{-\nu})exp(−e−ν); the paper calls it type 2, but the formula it states is the logit one. Integrating the rule over the shocks gives the multinomial logit probabilities:

Pr⁡(ai∣s)=exp⁡(vi(ai,s))∑k∈Aiexp⁡(vi(k,s))\Pr(a_i\mid\mathbf{s})=\frac{\exp\left(v_i(a_i,\mathbf{s})\right)}{\sum_{k\in A_i}\exp\left(v_i(k,\mathbf{s})\right)}Pr(ai​∣s)=∑k∈Ai​​exp(vi​(k,s))exp(vi​(ai​,s))​

Take logs. The denominator is the same for every action at a given state.

ln⁡Pr⁡(ai∣s)=vi(ai,s)−ln⁡∑k∈Aiexp⁡(vi(k,s))\ln\Pr(a_i\mid\mathbf{s})=v_i(a_i,\mathbf{s})-\ln\sum_{k\in A_i}\exp\left(v_i(k,\mathbf{s})\right)lnPr(ai​∣s)=vi​(ai​,s)−lnk∈Ai​∑​exp(vi​(k,s))

Write the same expression for ai′a_i'ai′​ and subtract; the log-sum term cancels.

ln⁡(Pr⁡(ai′∣s))−ln⁡(Pr⁡(ai∣s))=vi(ai′,s)−vi(ai,s)\ln\left(\Pr(a_i'\mid\mathbf{s})\right)-\ln\left(\Pr(a_i\mid\mathbf{s})\right)=v_i(a_i',\mathbf{s})-v_i(a_i,\mathbf{s})ln(Pr(ai′​∣s))−ln(Pr(ai​∣s))=vi​(ai′​,s)−vi​(ai​,s)

This is the Hotz and Miller inversion in its simplest form: log odds of observed choice frequencies equal differences in choice-specific values. The right-hand side contains the firm's entire dynamic problem, including the continuation value ViV_iVi​ and equilibrium beliefs about rivals, yet the left-hand side is a simple function of data. Only differences are identified, since adding a constant to every vi(⋅,s)v_i(\cdot,\mathbf{s})vi​(⋅,s) leaves all probabilities unchanged; with the normalization vi(0,s)=0v_i(0,\mathbf{s})=0vi​(0,s)=0 one gets vi(ai,s)=ln⁡Pr⁡(ai∣s)−ln⁡Pr⁡(0∣s)v_i(a_i,\mathbf{s})=\ln\Pr(a_i\mid\mathbf{s})-\ln\Pr(0\mid\mathbf{s})vi​(ai​,s)=lnPr(ai​∣s)−lnPr(0∣s). Because the logit distribution has no unknown parameters here (its scale is normalized), the inversion does not involve θ\thetaθ. With other distributions the same logic applies with a different link, for example the normal one in equation (23).

Under Assumption MC the policy σi(s,νi)\sigma_i(\mathbf{s},\nu_i)σi​(s,νi​) is increasing in the scalar shock νi\nu_iνi​; take it strictly increasing, so that it has an inverse σi−1(ai;s)\sigma_i^{-1}(a_i;\mathbf{s})σi−1​(ai​;s) in its second argument. Fi(ai∣s)=Pr⁡(σi(s,νi)≤ai∣s)F_i(a_i\mid\mathbf{s})=\Pr\left(\sigma_i(\mathbf{s},\nu_i)\leq a_i\mid\mathbf{s}\right)Fi​(ai​∣s)=Pr(σi​(s,νi​)≤ai​∣s)

Start from the recursion in equation (1), now with the dependence on θ\thetaθ made explicit, and substitute it into itself. The first line is an assumption on primitives: profit is an inner product of known basis functions Ψi=(ψi1,…,ψiM)\Psi_i=(\psi_i^1,\ldots,\psi_i^M)Ψi​=(ψi1​,…,ψiM​) and the parameter vector. Substitute it into equation (9).

Vi(s;σ;θ)=E[∑t=0∞βt Ψi(σ(st,νt),st,νit)⋅θ  ∣  s0=s;θ]V_i(\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\sigma};\theta)=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^t\,\Psi_i(\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{s}_t,\boldsymbol{\nu}_t),\mathbf{s}_t,\nu_{it})\cdot\theta\;\Big|\;\mathbf{s}_0=\mathbf{s};\theta\right]Vi​(s;σ;θ)=E[t=0∑∞​βtΨi​(σ(st​,νt​),st​,νit​)⋅θ​s0​=s;θ]

So the conditioning on θ\thetaθ can be dropped, and θ\thetaθ is a constant vector inside the expectation. The vector Wi\mathbf{W}_iWi​ is free of θ\thetaθ, so each policy is simulated once and every candidate θ\thetaθ costs one inner product. Three conditions carry the result and all are needed: linearity of πi\pi_iπi​ in θ\thetaθ, shock distributions free of θ\thetaθ (or reparameterized so, as with ait(μ+κωit)a_{it}(\mu+\kappa\omega_{it})ait​(μ+κωit​)), and policies and transitions that do not move with θ\thetaθ, which is exactly what the two-step approach delivers. A term with known coefficient is handled by a component of θ\thetaθ fixed at one, as with W3W^3W3 in equation (24) and W1W^1W1 in equation (28). The value difference in equation (12) inherits linearity, g=[Wi(s;σi,σ−i)−Wi(s;σi′,σ−i)]⋅θg=\left[\mathbf{W}_i(\mathbf{s};\sigma_i,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i})-\mathbf{W}_i(\mathbf{s};\sigma_i',\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i})\right]\cdot\thetag=[Wi​(s;σi​,σ−i​)−Wi​(s;σi′​,σ−i​)]⋅θ.

This defines the set of structural parameters that rationalize the observed behavior: θ\thetaθ belongs to Θ0(σ,P)\Theta_0(\boldsymbol{\sigma},P)Θ0​(σ,P) when the profile σ\boldsymbol{\sigma}σ satisfies the equilibrium condition in equation (2) for every firm iii, state s\mathbf{s}s and alternative strategy σi′\sigma_i'σi′​, in the game whose transition is PPP and whose profits and shock distributions are indexed by θ\thetaθ. The arguments (σ,P)(\boldsymbol{\sigma},P)(σ,P) are the objects recovered in the first stage; the value functions on both sides are given by equation (9). Under Assumption ES the true θ0\theta_0θ0​ is in the set by construction.

The set is the model's identified set. If it is the single point θ0\theta_0θ0​ the model is point identified and the minimum distance estimator in equation (15) applies; if not, the bounds estimator in equation (19) targets a set. Nothing in the definition requires uniqueness of equilibrium: θ\thetaθ only has to make σ\boldsymbol{\sigma}σ one equilibrium.

In the linear case of equation (10) each condition reads

[Wi(s;σi,σ−i)−Wi(s;σi′,σ−i)]⋅θ≥0\left[\mathbf{W}_i(\mathbf{s};\sigma_i,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i})-\mathbf{W}_i(\mathbf{s};\sigma_i',\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i})\right]\cdot\theta\geq0[Wi​(s;σi​,σ−i​)−Wi​(s;σi′​,σ−i​)]⋅θ≥0

This also shows why some component of the payoff must have a known coefficient: if every element of θ\thetaθ were free, the inequalities would be homogeneous, θ=0\theta=0θ=0 would satisfy all of them and only directions could be learned. In the examples the scale is fixed by the known shock distribution (equation (24)) or by the static profit estimated in the first stage (equation (28)). Conditions at states never reached in the data cannot be evaluated and are dropped, which can only enlarge the set.

The function ggg is the gain from following the observed strategy instead of one particular deviation. Each index x=(i,s,σi′)x=(i,\mathbf{s},\sigma_i')x=(i,s,σi′​) picks a firm, a starting state and an alternative strategy; g(x;θ,α)g(x;\theta,\alpha)g(x;θ,α) is the value of firm iii at s\mathbf{s}s under the observed profile minus its value when it plays σi′\sigma_i'σi′​ and rivals keep σ−i\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i}σ−i​. The equilibrium condition in equations (2) and (11) for this xxx is g(x;θ,α)≥0g(x;\theta,\alpha)\geq0g(x;θ,α)≥0, and θ∈Θ0\theta\in\Theta_0θ∈Θ0​ exactly when g≥0g\geq0g≥0 for every xxx.

The two arguments play different roles. The parameter θ\thetaθ enters through profits and shock distributions. The first-stage parameter α\alphaα enters because the policy functions σj(s,νj;α)\sigma_j(\mathbf{s},\nu_j;\alpha)σj​(s,νj​;α) and the transition P(⋅∣⋅;α)P(\cdot\mid\cdot;\alpha)P(⋅∣⋅;α) that generate the paths in equation (9) are indexed by it; this is the slight abuse of notation the paper mentions, since α\alphaα appears in ViV_iVi​ only through σ\boldsymbol{\sigma}σ and PPP. Sampling error in α^n\hat{\alpha}_nα^n​ therefore shifts ggg, and this is the only source of asymptotic variance in equation (17).

In the linear case of equation (10),

g(x;θ,α)=[Wi(s;σi,σ−i;α)−Wi(s;σi′,σ−i;α)]⋅θg(x;\theta,\alpha)=\left[\mathbf{W}_i(\mathbf{s};\sigma_i,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i};\alpha)-\mathbf{W}_i(\mathbf{s};\sigma_i',\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{-i};\alpha)\right]\cdot\thetag(x;θ,α)=[Wi​(s;σi​,σ−i​;α)−Wi​(s;σi′​,σ−i​;α)]⋅θ

so ggg is linear in θ\thetaθ with a gradient that is a difference of two simulated vectors. The simulated analog g^\hat{g}g^​ replaces each ViV_iVi​ by its forward-simulation average; using the same shock draws for both terms makes them positively correlated and reduces the variance of the difference. The definition matches the paper's. A deviation σi′\sigma_i'σi′​ is informative only where it changes behavior; for a small perturbation of a continuous control, ggg at the truth is of second order in the size of the perturbation, because the observed policy satisfies a first-order condition.

The population criterion turns the system of inequalities g(x;θ,α)≥0g(x;\theta,\alpha)\geq0g(x;θ,α)≥0 into a single number. For each condition xxx the integrand is

(min⁡{g,0})2={0if g≥0g2if g<0\left(\min\left\{g,0\right\}\right)^2=\begin{cases}0 & \text{if } g\geq0\\ g^2 & \text{if } g<0\end{cases}(min{g,0})2={0g2​if g≥0if g<0​

so a satisfied inequality contributes nothing, however slack it is, and a violated one is penalized by the square of the violation. The distribution HHH over X\mathcal{X}X weights the conditions; it is chosen by the researcher (which firms, states and deviations to look at) and is not a feature of the data.

Three properties follow. First, Q≥0Q\geq0Q≥0, and Q(θ,α)=0Q(\theta,\alpha)=0Q(θ,α)=0 exactly when g≥0g\geq0g≥0 for HHH-almost every xxx. Since θ0\theta_0θ0​ satisfies every equilibrium condition, Q(θ0,α0)=0Q(\theta_0,\alpha_0)=0Q(θ0​,α0​)=0, the global minimum. Second, if θ0\theta_0θ0​ is the only parameter satisfying the inequalities in the support of HHH, then Q(θ,α0)>0Q(\theta,\alpha_0)>0Q(θ,α0​)>0 for θ≠θ0\theta\neq\theta_0θ=θ0​, which is the identification condition S2(iv). Third, the penalty h(y)=(min⁡{y,0})2h(y)=(\min\{y,0\})^2h(y)=(min{y,0})2 is continuously differentiable with h′(y)=2min⁡{y,0}h'(y)=2\min\{y,0\}h′(y)=2min{y,0}, so where differentiation under the integral is allowed,

∂∂θQ(θ,α)=2∫min⁡{g(x;θ,α),0}∂g(x;θ,α)∂θ dH(x)\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}Q(\theta,\alpha)=2\int\min\left\{g(x;\theta,\alpha),0\right\}\frac{\partial g(x;\theta,\alpha)}{\partial\theta}\,dH(x)∂θ∂​Q(θ,α)=2∫min{g(x;θ,α),0}∂θ∂g(x;θ,α)​dH(x)

which is zero at (θ0,α0)(\theta_0,\alpha_0)(θ0​,α0​) term by term. The second derivative of hhh is 2 for y<0y<0y<0, 0 for y>0y>0y>0 and does not exist at y=0y=0y=0; this kink matters for equation (16).

Squaring one-sided violations is the natural moment-inequality analog of least squares. In the linear case ggg is linear in θ\thetaθ and hhh is convex, so QQQ is convex in θ\thetaθ. The form matches the paper's definition; the sample version is equation (14).

This is the feasible version of the criterion in equation (13), with two substitutions. The integral over HHH becomes an average over nIn_InI​ conditions X1,…,XnIX_1,\ldots,X_{n_I}X1​,…,XnI​​, each a triple (firm, state, alternative strategy) drawn by the researcher from HHH. And the unknown ggg of equation (12) becomes g^\hat{g}g^​, in which both value functions are replaced by forward-simulation averages over nsn_sns​ paths, as described after equation (9). The form (average of squared negative parts, normalized by nIn_InI​) agrees with the paper's equation (5).

Three sample sizes are in play: nnn, the number of first-stage observations behind α^n\hat{\alpha}_nα^n​; nIn_InI​, the number of inequalities; and nsn_sns​, the number of simulated paths per inequality. Only nnn is limited by data. The criterion is evaluated at α=α^n\alpha=\hat{\alpha}_nα=α^n​ in equation (15), so first-stage error enters through g^\hat{g}g^​.

Because the penalty is nonlinear, simulation error does not average out exactly. With h(y)=(min⁡{y,0})2h(y)=(\min\{y,0\})^2h(y)=(min{y,0})2 convex and g^\hat{g}g^​ unbiased for ggg, Jensen's inequality gives

E[h(g^)]≥h(E[g^])=h(g)\mathbb{E}\left[h(\hat{g})\right]\geq h\left(\mathbb{E}[\hat{g}]\right)=h(g)E[h(g^​)]≥h(E[g^​])=h(g)

so each term of QnQ_nQn​ is biased upward by an amount of the order of the variance of g^\hat{g}g^​, that is of order 1/ns1/n_s1/ns​. This is the simulation bias that Assumption S2(iii) controls by requiring n/ns2→0n/n_s^2\rightarrow0n/ns2​→0. The same nonlinearity applied to first-stage noise is the source of the finite-sample bias in the scrap value seen in the Monte Carlo.

In the linear case g^(Xk;θ,α)=ΔW^k⋅θ\hat{g}(X_k;\theta,\alpha)=\Delta\hat{\mathbf{W}}_k\cdot\thetag^​(Xk​;θ,α)=ΔW^k​⋅θ, where ΔW^k\Delta\hat{\mathbf{W}}_kΔW^k​ is the difference of the two simulated Wi\mathbf{W}_iWi​ vectors for inequality kkk. Then QnQ_nQn​ is a convex, piecewise quadratic function of θ\thetaθ that can be evaluated at any θ\thetaθ without further simulation.

The estimator is the parameter value at which the estimated policies come closest to being mutual best responses: it minimizes the sample criterion of equation (14) with the first-stage estimate α^n\hat{\alpha}_nα^n​ plugged in. It is a two-step extremum estimator. The first step fixes policies and transitions; the second step searches over θ\thetaθ only, and never solves for an equilibrium.

When the minimum is interior, θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ satisfies the first-order condition

∂∂θQn(θ^,α^n)=2nI∑k=1nImin⁡{g^(Xk;θ^,α^n),0}∂g^(Xk;θ^,α^n)∂θ=0\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}Q_n(\hat{\theta},\hat{\alpha}_n)=\frac{2}{n_I}\sum_{k=1}^{n_I}\min\left\{\hat{g}(X_k;\hat{\theta},\hat{\alpha}_n),0\right\}\frac{\partial\hat{g}(X_k;\hat{\theta},\hat{\alpha}_n)}{\partial\theta}=0∂θ∂​Qn​(θ^,α^n​)=nI​2​k=1∑nI​​min{g^​(Xk​;θ^,α^n​),0}∂θ∂g^​(Xk​;θ^,α^n​)​=0

Only the inequalities violated at θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ appear, each weighted by the size of its violation: the estimator balances the violated conditions against one another. In the linear case ∂g^/∂θ=ΔW^k\partial\hat{g}/\partial\theta=\Delta\hat{\mathbf{W}}_k∂g^​/∂θ=ΔW^k​, the difference of the simulated Wi\mathbf{W}_iWi​ vectors, and the problem is a convex piecewise quadratic program. This first-order condition is the starting point for the expansion in equation (16) and the limit distribution in equation (17).

In the population the minimized value is zero. In a finite sample the minimum of QnQ_nQn​ is usually positive, because noise in α^n\hat{\alpha}_nα^n​ and in the simulation makes some inequalities fail at every θ\thetaθ; then θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ does not make the estimated policies an exact equilibrium. Identification comes from the deviations that are close to profitable: a deviation that loses by a wide margin at all plausible θ\thetaθ never binds and carries no information, which is why the choice of HHH affects precision.

When several parameter values satisfy the equilibrium inequalities, the target is the set ΘnI(σ,P)\Theta_{n_I}(\boldsymbol{\sigma},P)ΘnI​​(σ,P) of all θ\thetaθ that satisfy the nIn_InI​ fixed conditions, and a single minimizer of the criterion is not meaningful. The construction follows Manski and Tamer (2002) and matches the paper's equation (6).

Each ingredient has a job. Subtracting the minimum makes the set nonempty even when noise keeps QnQ_nQn​ strictly positive everywhere, as usually happens in finite samples. The slack μn>0\mu_n>0μn​>0 protects against the opposite error. In the population, QQQ equals zero on the whole identified set, so the sample criterion is flat there up to noise; the exact argmin of QnQ_nQn​ would then pick out an arbitrary small part of the set, driven by noise. Keeping all near-minimizers retains every point whose criterion is statistically indistinguishable from the minimum. Letting μn→0\mu_n\rightarrow0μn​→0 keeps points outside the identified set, where Q>0Q>0Q>0, from surviving in the limit.

This is the critical value used to build the confidence region of equation (22), following Romano and Shaikh (2006a). For a fixed candidate θ\thetaθ, the test statistic is the scaled criterion n⋅Qn(θ,α^n)n\cdot Q_n(\theta,\hat{\alpha}_n)n⋅Qn​(θ,α^n​), and its distribution under the hypothesis that θ\thetaθ is in the identified set is approximated by subsampling: draw BBB subsamples of size nbn_bnb​ from the data, recompute the criterion on each to obtain Qn,bQ_{n,b}Qn,b​, and scale by nbn_bnb​. The scaling is by sample size, not its square root, because the criterion is a squared distance. At a θ\thetaθ in the identified set, an inequality that binds has g^\hat{g}g^​ of order n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 from first-stage error, so (min⁡{g^,0})2(\min\{\hat{g},0\})^2(min{g^​,0})2 is of order 1/n1/n1/n and n⋅Qnn\cdot Q_nn⋅Qn​ has a nondegenerate limit; inequalities that hold strictly contribute nothing asymptotically. The limit is not a standard distribution and depends on which inequalities bind at θ\thetaθ, which is why it is approximated by resampling and why the critical value varies with θ\thetaθ. Subsampling, unlike the bootstrap, remains valid for such nonsmooth statistics, provided nb→∞n_b\rightarrow\inftynb​→∞ and nb/n→0n_b/n\rightarrow0nb​/n→0.

The inequality, in place of equality, allows for atoms in JθJ_\thetaJθ​; for instance if no inequality binds at θ\thetaθ the statistic and the critical value are both zero in the limit and coverage tends to one. The statement is pointwise: it holds for each fixed θ\thetaθ in the identified set, in particular for θ0\theta_0θ0​, but it does not say that the whole set is covered with probability 0.95. Covering the whole set requires replacing the statistic by its supremum over the set, as in the step-down procedure, and gives a larger region. These two expressions specify the investment technology, following Pakes and McGuire (1994). An incumbent that spends Iit≥0I_{it}\geq0Iit​≥0 sees its quality ziz_izi​ rise by one step next period with probability ρIit/(1+ρIit)\rho I_{it}/(1+\rho I_{it})ρIit​/(1+ρIit​) and stay unchanged otherwise; the parameter ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0 measures the effectiveness of investment. The probability is zero at Iit=0I_{it}=0Iit​=0, increasing and strictly concave, and approaches one only as investment grows without bound, so there are diminishing returns and no certain success. Its derivative is ρ/(1+ρIit)2\rho/(1+\rho I_{it})^2ρ/(1+ρIit​)2. With the true value ρ=1.25\rho=1.25ρ=1.25, investing one unit succeeds with probability 1.25/2.251.25/2.251.25/2.25, about 0.56. Independently, the outside good improves with probability δ\deltaδ, which erodes every incumbent's relative position.
